items.title: The Benefits of Reading Are Incalculable
items.summary: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. The next wellness craze is reading, my colleague Sophie Haigney reported in The Atlantic this week . She tried a new app called Readwise Books, which tracks a user’s words-per-minute the way a health app might track their mileage or heart rate. This is just one example of how influencers and the health-conscious have recently been making “a case for reading’s value that sounds a lot like the way we talk about physical health,” Haigney wrote. The fitness challenge 75 Hard, she noted, doesn’t just prescribe workouts and a specific water intake. It also requires participants to read “10 pages of nonfiction a day.” But it offers no guidance about what those titles should be or how to discern the value of any given 10-page chunk. More confusing to me was a claim, from the bodybuilder and former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, that picking up books is “a low-risk behavior (really, there’s no risk in reading more).” First, here are 6 new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section: One word to explain America Welcome to the era of second-screen reading The loneliness of buying too many things The writer who made food fun “Long Wave,” a short story by Daisy Johnson “Caravaggio,” a poem by Peter Balakian That stopped me in my tracks. No risk? If Schwarzenegger, or any other literature-as-wellbeing influencer, truly believes that the activity is as powerful as they say it is, how can that be true? Written language is so central to our society because it can, and does, lead to real action. If printed matter has the potential to change stubborn minds, inspire the most unlikely empathy, and transmit the wildest human ideas, then perusing 10 pages of a hateful manifesto could, under the right circumstances, entail a lot of risk. I don’t mean to make an argument for locking away dangerous ideas or for thinking of books as vectors of unwholesome thoughts. Instead, like Haigney, I’m skeptical of anyone who posits reading as a harmless, vaguely healthful behavior akin to eating vegetables or wearing sunscreen. I think that people arguing for reading as a practice of personal and spiritual transformation should follow their premise to its conclusions: Books can alter a life, undermine foundational beliefs, even change the world. Tracking one’s reading as if it were a workout shortchanges its power. What debates over the end of literacy sometimes miss is that the content of a book is far more important than any metric—whether words-per-minute or year-over-year sales. I’ve argued this before , when I encouraged people to measure themselves not by statistics but instead by qualitative benchmarks: “Finish Anna Karenina ” is a more meaningful goal than “turn 900 pages.” Slipping and sliding across 3,200 frictionless pages of A Court of Thorns and Roses feels like a wholly different exercise than the deliberate, engaged immersion of Edward P. Jones’s The Known World . And neither is going to improve my VO2 max—which is fine by me, because that’s not why I’m reading them. Illustration by Steph Wu / The Atlantic. Source: Getty. Let’s Not Make Reading a Wellness Trend By Sophie Haigney Books have long been considered morally and intellectually virtuous. Now some influencers are claiming that they’re good for your physical health. Read the full article. What to Read The Invisible Kingdom , by Meghan O’Rourke The best memoirs are those that take an occurrence, a life, or a history that is not our own, and so fully transport the reader into the world of the writer that our capacity for empathy expands in ways we could not have imagined. That is the experience I had reading O’Rourke’s The Invisible Kingdom , in which she writes beautifully and honestly about living with a chronic, mysterious, and often debilitating illness. Some of my loved ones live with their own enigmatic, ongoing health issues, and this book provided me with insight and context with which to more fully understand their experiences. O’Rourke places her life in conversation with the larger body of historical research on chronic illness, to provide a narrative that is both deeply personal and deeply investigated. In the age of COVID, when so many across the world are still living with the lingering, enervating symptoms of the virus, the lessons and stories here are becoming more relevant to all of us—just as they were for me. — Clint Smith From our list: A book that changed how I think Out Next Week 📚 Long Wave , by Daisy Johnson 📚 Arlington: An African American History , by William A. Blair 📚 Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir , by Bob Woodward Your Weekend Read Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic The Least Productive Day of the Year By Sophia Nguyen Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off. First, she chalked it up to “personal reasons.” Then she said her birthday was coming up. But eventually, she came clean: She wanted to play Grand Theft Auto VI right when the game dropped, on November 19. Rogers had big plans—decorating with neon lights, stocking up on energy drinks, adorning those drinks with little paper umbrellas. She and her fiancé were going to play until their eyes gave out. Read the full article. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic . items.title: Did men evolve to fight each other? Scientists can’t agree.
items.summary: Anthropologist David Puts was a graduate student trying to decide on a dissertation topic when inspiration struck him at a mall food court. While eating a cheeseburger, he overheard two men behind him speaking in unusually deep voices. “I turned around to see what was happening, and there was a young, good-looking female nearby,” Puts said. His initial thought was that human males evolved deep voices to attract women, but he soon began to wonder whether they might also help establish dominance over other men: “A deep voice is intimidating — think about Darth Vader.” So, for his dissertation, Puts tested both possibilities. What he found surprised him. Women tended to prefer a deeper, more masculine voice, but the effect of voice pitch on their ratings of male attractiveness wasn’t very big. Meanwhile, the effect of voice pitch on men’s judgment of another man’s dominance and fighting ability was 15 times bigger. The unexpected result led Puts to revisit earlier studies. He noticed that “the literature was really biased towards female mate choice” as a reason for deep voices, while findings related to male-male competition seemed to get “pushed under the rug.” This realization became the foundation for Puts’ theory that competition between males for mates, also known as “male-male contest competition,” may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized. Puts, now a professor of anthropology and psychology at Pennsylvania State University, has continued to think about and develop this theory ever since the seed for it was planted in his brain in that mall food court in the early 2000s. Although he said he is mostly driven by a fascination with human nature, there’s more to his theory than pure academic interest. He believes that evolutionary understanding might help explain aspects of male psychology and inform positive social change. Competition between males for mates may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized. In November 2026, Puts and graduate student Saeed Koohgard published a review titled “ The deadliest primate: Contest competition and the evolution of human males ” in the Journal of Human Evolution . The review links modern-day male characteristics, including physical aggression, to male-male contest competition among our ancestors — a controversial theory. “This [idea] is supported primarily by evolutionary psychologists,” said Agustín Fuentes, an anthropologist at Princeton University. “Most anthropologists do not support this at all.” He said that those interested in understanding male violence should read the paper “but recognize this is a very teeny slice and a very biased view” in the midst of the wider anthropological, psychological, and sociological literature. The ancestral mating system For at least the past 150,000 years, the effective number of reproducing women at any given time has been roughly three times that of men, according to a 2015 study looking at Y-chromosome and mitochondrial DNA. This may reflect male invaders displacing local men, but Puts and Koohgard think it points to a polygynous mating system, where some men fathered children with several partners, while many other men had no children at all. They believe that our ancestors lived in single-male family units embedded within larger bands, as hamadryas and gelada baboons do. This setup meant that “our male ancestors intensely fought, threatened, and killed each other to monopolize mates,” Puts said. In their review, Puts and Koohgard cite several findings that are consistent with their theory. For example, in a study of Eurasian Neanderthal and early modern human remains from 80,000 to 20,000 years ago, men were about six times more likely than women to show signs of head injuries . Furthermore, a study of homicide data spanning two decades and four locations (Canada, England/Wales, Chicago, and Detroit) found that unrelated men kill each other 27 times more often than unrelated women kill each other . “A lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.” David Puts Puts and Koohgard also point to several features of the male anatomy as complementary evidence of male-male contest competition. Men are larger than women on average, with 61% more muscle mass overall and 75% more upper-body muscle mass. Size and muscularity are traits that help win fights. Men also have what biologists call “badges of status,” such as facial hair and deep voices. These traits signal dominance and help to win resources, such as mates, without engaging in costly fights. Puts and Koohgard argue that, together, these lines of evidence suggest that male-male contest competition has played an important role in shaping men’s behaviors, including physical aggression. People might hear this theory and misread it as a justification of male violence, Puts said, but he stresses that understanding evolutionary influences is not the same as condoning violence — the idea that something being natural or evolved makes it justified is what’s known as the “naturalistic fallacy.” Although Puts and Koohgard’s theory centers on the idea that aggression helped our male ancestors to win mates, Puts doubts that the most violent males were ever the most successful. “There are huge costs to violence,” he said, “and if you’re living in a group and you’re a belligerent loose cannon, you’re likely to be killed or at least ostracized.” Instead, Puts thinks that “a lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.” Clashing views Fuentes is not convinced by Puts and Koohgard’s theory. The claim of a polygynous ancestral mating system is “highly disputed,” he said, and the “vast majority of geneticists who work in this area” conclude that our ancestors were most likely monogamous, with some mild polygyny. He accused Puts and Koohgard of selectively citing works that support their theory while leaving out research that complicates or challenges it — their paper doesn’t mention Nam Kim and Marc Kissel ’s book Emergent Warfare in Our Evolutionary Past , for example. That book frames violence as complex and dependent on multiple conditions — not simply an evolved male strategy. Citing it would make it “more complicated to make the argument that [they’re] making,” Fuentes said. However, Raymond Hames, an emeritus professor of anthropology at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, praised Puts and Koohgard’s review as “very comprehensive.” He said the paper’s strength is that it tests several alternative hypotheses that might explain male traits, such as sexual division of labor, and finds them a poor fit. His only objection is to the paper’s title: “The deadliest primate.” “Although we are violent, we are not the deadliest of all primates,” Hames said. Red-tailed monkeys, blue monkeys, and red-fronted lemurs are all far more likely than humans to kill their own kind, according to a 2016 study . “Humans didn’t evolve to punch each other — our hands are horrible at it. Our bodies actually aren’t that great for violence, but our minds are.” Agustín Fuentes With regard to Fuentes’ point, Hames thinks that warfare, or coalitionary violence, and one-on-one male violence aren’t interchangeable.
